summary:
Today's health-tech landscape shows momentum across multiple fronts despite regulatory adjustments. Medicaid work requirements enforcement has been delayed six months to July 2027, while Democrats are coalescing around proposals to expand Medicare eligibility, signaling ongoing policy shifts around healthcare access. On the venture capital side, Zus Health secured $33 million in Series B funding to improve healthcare connectivity, and Windward Bio raised $225 million in its IPO for next-generation antibody drugs with backing from Sanofi, reflecting continued investor confidence in health-tech and biotech innovation.

Clinical AI is making tangible operational gains, with Corewell Health's ambient AI reducing nursing documentation by 52 percent and AI systems demonstrating improved accuracy in delirium detection, while partnerships like Dyania Health and NVIDIA's work on patient record analysis signal deeper AI integration into care delivery. The Trump administration is committing up to $4.9 million toward ibogaine research for PTSD treatment, marking a notable investment in psychedelic-assisted therapies.

Several investigative stories are raising governance concerns: questions linger around Boston Scientific's Watchman marketing practices relative to supporting evidence, Oura's acquisition of a telehealth company is creating potential conflicts of interest involving Eli Lilly, and senators are introducing a bill to address financial conflicts among preventive care panel members. Meanwhile, a STAT investigation found unproven "three-parent IVF" procedures being marketed to older women through fertility tourism clinics, highlighting quality and safety gaps in less-regulated segments.
